summary: Specifies a base profile for X.509 v3 certificates and v2 CRLs for use with the US National Security Agency's Suite B cryptography. It assumes the reader knows RFC 5280. Its status is historic.

eli5.summary: Governments use a specific set of cryptography choices. This document defines the certificate rules for that set. It is now historic.

questions: what is the suite b certificate profile
suite b elliptic curves p-256 p-384
subtitle: Certificate and CRL profiles for using NSA's Suite B cryptography with elliptic curve algorithms.

tldr.problem: The NSA's Suite B cryptography standard specifies approved algorithms, but X.509 certificates and CRLs (Certificate Revocation Lists) needed a clear profile defining how to use those algorithms within the RFC 5280 framework.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies which elliptic curves (P-256, P-384), signature algorithms (ECDSA with SHA-256 or SHA-384), and certificate extensions are required for Suite B implementations, along with specific rules for CAs, self-signed certificates, and end-entity certificates.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5759 is Historic because Suite B itself was superseded by Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite (CNSA Suite) for US government use.

facts.label: Signature algorithms
facts.value: ECDSA with SHA-256 or ECDSA with SHA-384

today: RFC 5759 is Historic. Suite B was the NSA's approved cryptography suite for protecting US government classified information, but it was superseded by the Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite (CNSA Suite) in 2015. CNSA Suite restricts to P-384 and removes Suite B's P-256 option, and uses SHA-384 as the primary hash.

sections.title: Suite B and Elliptic Curve Cryptography
sections.content:
The United States National Security Agency's Suite B Cryptography specifies a set of approved algorithms suitable for protecting classified information. Suite B uses elliptic curve cryptography (ECC) instead of RSA, providing equivalent security with smaller key sizes and better performance.

This RFC defines a base profile for X.509 v3 certificates and X.509 v2 Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) that implement Suite B. The profile builds on RFC 5280 (the base X.509 standard) but elevates some optional features to required status and restricts others. All Suite B certificates must use elliptic curve public keys and be signed with ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm).
sections.eli5: Suite B is a set of math tricks approved for secret government work. This document says how to write those math tricks into a digital certificate using a standard format.

sections.title: Allowed Curves, Signature Algorithms, and Hashes
sections.content:
Suite B specifies two elliptic curves: P-256 (secp256r1) and P-384 (secp384r1). Every Suite B certificate must contain either an ECDSA signing key or an ECDH (Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman) key agreement key on one of these curves. A signing CA's key must use the same curve as or a stronger curve than the certificate it signs: a CA with a P-256 key can sign certificates with P-256 keys, and a CA with a P-384 key can sign P-256 or P-384 certificates.

Signatures use ECDSA with either ecdsa-with-SHA256 (OID 1.2.840.10045.4.3.2) or ecdsa-with-SHA384 (OID 1.2.840.10045.4.3.3). The hash algorithm must match the curve strength: P-256 keys are hashed with SHA-256, and P-384 keys are hashed with SHA-384. The signature itself encodes the two ECDSA values (r and s) as ASN.1 INTEGERs within a SEQUENCE.
sections.eli5: Use one of two approved math curves for your key. Sign everything with a matching ECDSA signature and hash method: P-256 with SHA-256, or P-384 with SHA-384. Encode the signature as two numbers wrapped in the right way.

sections.title: Certificate Extensions and CA Requirements
sections.content:
Self-signed CA certificates (a CA's own root certificate) must include the subjectKeyIdentifier, keyUsage, and basicConstraints extensions. The keyUsage extension must be marked critical with keyCertSign and cRLSign bits set; digitalSignature and nonRepudiation bits are optional. The basicConstraints extension must be marked critical with the cA boolean set to true.

Non-self-signed CA certificates must include authorityKeyIdentifier, keyUsage, and basicConstraints extensions. If the CA has certificate policies to assert, certificatePolicies must be included and marked non-critical. End entity certificates (user or service certificates) must include authorityKeyIdentifier and keyUsage extensions; for signing certificates, keyUsage must mark digitalSignature, while for key agreement certificates, it must mark keyAgreement.
sections.eli5: Different types of certificates need different marks in their extensions. CA certificates need special marks saying they can sign other certificates. User certificates need marks saying whether they can sign or exchange keys. All the marks must follow strict rules.

sections.title: Public Key Encoding and Interoperability
sections.content:
Suite B public keys use the id-ecPublicKey algorithm identifier. The curve is specified using the namedCurve option (not the older specifiedCurve or implicitCurve options). For P-256, the OID is secp256r1; for P-384, it is secp384r1. The elliptic curve point itself (the public key value) is encoded as an OCTET STRING in either compressed or uncompressed form.

For interoperability, all Suite B implementations must be prepared to process the uncompressed point format, though compressed format is also acceptable. The OCTET STRING representation of the point is then mapped to a BIT STRING as the subjectPublicKey field. Communities using Suite B may further restrict these options—for example, requiring only uncompressed points—but these restrictions must not be assumed when communicating with other communities.
sections.eli5: Write the public key using standard formats and codes. Everyone must be able to read the uncompressed format, though a compressed format is also okay. Different groups might add their own stricter rules, but they still need to talk to each other using the basic format.

sections.title: CRL Signatures and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Suite B CRLs (Certificate Revocation Lists) follow the same signature rules as certificates: they must be signed with ECDSA using SHA-256 or SHA-384, matched to the issuing CA's key curve. The CRL signature generation follows the same rules as the certificate signature generation, including the same ASN.1 encoding for the r and s values.

The specification recommends that a single key pair not be used for both signature and key establishment operations, reducing the risk if one key is compromised. Since CRLs are public objects that must be periodically published and distributed, their signatures must be robust and widely understood. Communities implementing Suite B may define additional security policies, such as requiring longer path constraints, specific key sizes, or mandatory revocation checking.
sections.eli5: CRLs (lists of revoked certificates) are signed the same way as regular certificates. Do not use the same key for both signing and secret exchanges—keep them separate for safety.
